---
title: "Condition Numbers"
---

```{julia}
using DelimitedFiles, LinearAlgebra, StatsBase, StatsPlots
```

# Definition

Assume $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is nonsingular and consider the system of linear equation 

$$
\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

The solution is 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}  \mathbf{b}.
$$

We want to know how the solution changes with a small perturbation of the input $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{A}$).

Let 

$$
\mathbf{b}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{b} + \Delta \mathbf{b}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} (\mathbf{b} + \Delta \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}.
$$

It follows that

$$
\|\Delta \mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{A}^{-1} \Delta \mathbf{b}\| \le \|\mathbf{A}^{-1}\| \|\Delta \mathbf{b}\|
$$

for any matrix norm $\| \cdot \|$. Because $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$, $\|\mathbf{b}\| \le \|\mathbf{A}\| \|\mathbf{x}\|$ and

$$
\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} \le \|\mathbf{A}\| \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{b}\|}.
$$

This yields

$$
\frac{ \|\Delta \mathbf{x}\|}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} \le \|\mathbf{A}\|\|\mathbf{A}^{-1}\| \frac{\|\Delta \mathbf{b}\|}{\|\mathbf{b}\|}.
$$

The quantity $\kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \|\mathbf{A}\| \|\mathbf{A}^{-1}\|$ is known as the **condition number for linear equation**. It depends on the matrix norm being used. For example, $\kappa_p$ means condition number defined from matrix-$p$ norm. **Large condition numbers are "bad".**

# Facts about $\kappa(\mathbf{A})$

Some facts about condition numbers:

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
\kappa(\mathbf{A}) &=& \kappa(\mathbf{A}^{-1})	\\
\kappa(c\mathbf{A}) &=& \kappa(\mathbf{A})	\\
\kappa(\mathbf{A}) &\ge& 1	\\
%\kappa_1(\mathbf{A}) &=& \kappa_\infty (\mathbf{A}^T)	\\
\kappa_2 (\mathbf{A}) &=& \kappa_2 (\mathbf{A}^T) = \frac{\sigma_1(\mathbf{A})}{\sigma_n(\mathbf{A})}	\\
\kappa_2(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A}) &=& \frac{\lambda_1(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A})}{\lambda_n(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A})} =  \kappa_2^2(\mathbf{A}) \ge \kappa_2(\mathbf{A}).
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

- Here $\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{A})$ denotes the $i$-th *singular value* of $\mathbf{A}$, ordered as $\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{A}) \ge \sigma_{2}(\mathbf{A}) \ge \ldots \ge \sigma_{n}(\mathbf{A})$.
- The last fact says that the condition number of $\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A}$ can be much larger than that of $\mathbf{A}$.
- The smallest singular value $\sigma_n$ measures the _distance to trouble_.

# Application to Regression

The **condition number for the least squares problem** is more complicated. Roughly speaking, 

- methods based on normal equations (Cholesky, sweep) have a condition number depending on $[\kappa_2(\mathbf{X})]^2$
- QR for a _small norm_ least squares problem has a condition depending on $\kappa_2(\mathbf{X})$; i.e. solution to 

    $$
    \mathrm{minimize}~\|\mathbf{x}\| \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}
    $$
    

Consider the simple case

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
	\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
	1 & 1 \\
	10^{-3} & 0 \\
	0 & 10^{-3}
	\end{pmatrix}.
\end{eqnarray*}
$$
Forming normal equations yields a singular Gramian matrix
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
	\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
	1 & 1 \\
	1 & 1
	\end{pmatrix}
\end{eqnarray*}
$$
if executed with a precision of 6 decimal digits.

# Julia Implementation

The Julia function [`cond`](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/stdlib/LinearAlgebra/#LinearAlgebra.cond) computes $\kappa_p$ for $p=1$, 2 (default), or $\infty$.

# Longley Example

The [Longley (1967)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2283673?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents) macroeconomic data set is a famous test example for numerical software in the early days.

```{julia}
longley = readdlm(joinpath("assets", "longley.txt"))
```


```{julia}
corrplot(longley, 
  label = ["Employ" "Price" "GNP" "Jobless" "Military" "PopSize" "Year"],
  xrotation = 45,
  size = (1000, 800)
)
```

Let's regress `Employment` on other variables:

```{julia}
# response: Employment
y = longley[:, 1]

# predictor matrix
X = [ones(length(y)) longley[:, 2:end]]
```

```{julia}
cond(X)
```

```{julia}
# we see the smallest singular value (aka trouble number) is very small
xsvals = svdvals(X)
```

```{julia}
# condition number of the design matrix
xcond = maximum(xsvals) / minimum(xsvals)
```

```{julia}
# X is full rank from SVD
xrksvd = rank(X)
```

```{julia}
# least squares from QR
X \ y
```

```{julia}
# Gram matrix
G = X'X
```

```{julia}
# rank of Gram matrix from SVD
# rank deficient! We lost precision when forming Gram matrix
rank(G)
```

```{julia}
svdvals(G)
```

```{julia}
# rank of Gram matrix from cholesky
# full!
gchol = cholesky(Symmetric(G), Val(true))
rank(gchol)
```

```{julia}
# least squares solution from Cholesky matches those from QR
gchol \ (X'y)
```

Now let us re-run above example using **single precision**.

```{julia}
Xsp = Float32.(X)
ysp = Float32.(y)

# least squares by QR: dramatically different from Float64 solution
Xsp \ ysp
```

```{julia}
# least squares by Cholesky: failed
G = Xsp'Xsp
gchol = cholesky(Symmetric(G), Val(true), check=false)
gchol \ (Xsp'ysp)
```

```{julia}
rank(Xsp)
```

```{julia}
# rank of Gram matrix by Cholesky
rank(gchol)
```

```{julia}
# rank of Gram matrix by SVD
rank(G)
```

**Standardizing the predictors** improves the condition number.

```{julia}
# center and standardize matrix along dimension 1
Xcs = zscore(X[:, 2:end], 1)
Xcs = [ones(length(y)) Xcs]
```

```{julia}
cond(Xcs)
```

```{julia}
rank(Xcs)
```

```{julia}
rank(Xcs'Xcs)
```
